newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Communists hit at Jospin over Renault plant.
newsitem.headline: French Communists hit at Jospin over Renault plant.

text.p: France's Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin came under fire on Sunday from his Communist cabinet partners who demanded that he freeze carmaker Renault's decision to close down its 3,100-worker Belgian plant.

As Jospin faced angry criticism from unions and from within his own party, Paul Lespagnol, a member of the Communist Party's national secretariat, asked Jospin to declare a moratorium on Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer's decision.
Louis Bocquet, the Communist floor leader in the National Assembly, said the plant's future was in the hands of the state, which is the main Renault shareholder with a 46 percent stake.
"The state...decides. The government has the means to keep the Vilvoorde plant open," he told a public meeting in the northern region bordering Belgium.

The loss-making French carmaker said on Saturday it was going ahead with the closure of the Vilvoorde plant, first announced five months ago under a conservative government, after an independent report failed to find any viable alternative.
"Jospin has not kept his promises," the Communist-led CGT union said, adding that Renault staff and French and European public opinion would not let Jospin and Schweitzer off the hook.

The controversial Vilvoorde closure was the second issue threatening to drive a wedge between the Socialists and the Communists who hold three portfolios in the cabinet appointed after the Left's June 1 parliamentary election victory.
Hardline Communist MP Maxime Gremetz accused Jospin of reneging on what he said had been a pre-election accord with the Communists to raise the minimum wage by eight percent.

"This is what the Communists have agreed upon in order to take part in government," he told the weekly Journal du Dimanche. Gremetz abstained in a confidence vote earlier this month after Jospin announced a four percent minimum wage rise.

Conservatives also hit at Jospin. "It took less than a month to wipe out for ever the legend of this prime minister who says what he does and does what he says," said Philippe Seguin, who is to take over the Gaullist main opposition party next month.
Centre-right former education minister Francois Bayrou said Jospin would be unable to keep many of his promises. "I believe there will be a lot of disappointment," he said.

Junior Industry Minister Christian Pierret said the plant's fate was sealed under the conservative government, and Jospin has kept a campaign pledge to order an independent report on the plant and win better redundancy conditions for the workers.

"No-one will be left on the roadside," he told the Journal du Dimanche. "If the free market had prevailed, as for example in Britain and the United States, the workers would have been summarily thrown out onto the street."
The pro-Socialist CFDT union said the report commissioned by Renault had amounted to "an alibi for the public authorities".
A Renault spokeswoman said the closure could be pushed back from July 31 to October and talks would continue on redundancy payments and job offers to workers at other Renault factories.

Ex-Socialist Party leader Henri Emmanuelli, a member of the party's left wing, vowed to keep fighting to prevent the closure and said he would raise the issue with Socialist members of the National Assembly. The Socialist floor leader Jean-Marc Ayrault said the closure was inescapable but the government would fight to bring another form of industrial activity at Vilvoorde.
Belgian unionists occupying the Vilvoorde plant announced a toughening of their protest and said they were holding as a "war treasure" 5,300 Megane cars assembled at the plant.
"The French Socialists did not keep their word. The policy remains unchanged despite the government changeover," said Karel Gacoms of Belgium's FGTB union.
